title: Vidyasagar and the dharma of an age
word: with the Keeper's framing of what
hookLine: a law book that hands each age its own rules, and an argument over a widow's second marriage
carry: each age has its own dharma: yuga dharma
tomorrow: what does a handful of rice by the back door have to do with Manu?

lines: A RULE THAT MADE SENSE ONCE.
cards: Every family has a rule that made sense once: back before dark, no swimming after lunch, no phones at the table. Sooner or later someone asks whether it still holds. The Hindu dharma books asked that about themselves.
And one argument over it, about whether a widow may marry again, was fought line by line, with both sides quoting scripture.

teach.b: Start with the idea both sides shared. The Manusmriti's first chapter says time turns through four ages, and that people's duties differ from age to age. The Parashara Smriti goes further.
In paraphrase: Manu's laws for the first age, Gautama's for the second, Shankha and Likhita's for the third, and Parashara's for the Kali age, the one tradition says we live in now.
That's yuga dharma, the dharma of an age. Now the debate. On one side, Ishvarchandra Vidyasagar, a scholar in Bengal.
His case: if Parashara is the book for this age, listen to Parashara.

And Parashara has a verse that lets a woman take another husband when hers is missing, has died, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has been cast out. So widows may remarry, inside the tradition's own law.
On the other side, his opponents, also reading closely.

Their best case: one verse shouldn't overturn what households had kept for generations; other books and other readings point the other way; and if each age can rewrite the rules, who decides which rule has run out?
That question is a real one, and it's still asked. In Vidyasagar's lifetime the law changed, and widows were allowed to remarry.
Both sides took the books seriously. What divided them was who gets to say what this age needs.
That's still the question in many Hindu homes, when a grandparent's rule meets a grandchild's life: is this dharma itself, or the dharma of an age?

how: Hindu teachers sometimes speak of yuga dharma, the duties fit for an age, when explaining why some rules in the old dharma books are no longer followed; Vidyasagar's case for widow remarriage rested on the Parashara Smriti.

games.q: what does “with the keeper's framing of what” mean?
o: the order of seats at a family festival meal
a vow taken at the start of each new age
what a tradition holds on to, and what it drops

games.q: one argument, two sides — tap the pairs.
p: the law book for the Kali age
argued for widows from the texts
who decides which rule ran out?

s: reformers like Vidyasagar threw the old books out
he argued from inside them, quoting Parashara, the book tradition gives to this age.
a dharma book itself places Manu's laws in an earlier age
the Parashara Smriti gives Manu's laws to the first age and its own to the Kali age.

games.q: you're asked to give Vidyasagar's opponents their best case, fairly. which line is theirs?
o: if each age can rewrite the rules, who decides which rule has run out?
Parashara is the law book for this age, so follow Parashara.
the old books don't matter at all anymore.
games.why: that's their strongest question, and it's still asked. Vidyasagar's answer was Parashara, the book tradition gives to this age.

practice: Bring to mind someone in your family who keeps an old rule you've never understood. In your head, or on your phone, write them one short, curious question about why they keep it, with no argument hidden inside.
You don't have to send it; let the question sit with you until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Kept and rejected, by the age: yuga dharma, the idea that each age has its own dharma, and the hard question of who decides.

orig.note: Sanskrit yuga dharma, the dharma of an age: duties fit for their time.

carryVoice: Pocket this: each age has its own dharma, yuga dharma, and Vidyasagar argued it line by line, from inside the books. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Manusmriti 1.81–1.86 (the four ages; the duties of people differ from age to age, 1.85)
Parashara Smriti 1.24 (Manu's laws for the Krita age, Gautama's for the Treta, Shankha and Likhita's for the Dvapara, Parashara's for the Kali)
Parashara Smriti 4.30 (a woman may take another husband when hers is missing, dead, a renunciant, impotent or cast out)
Ishvarchandra Vidyasagar, treatise on the remarriage of Hindu widows (his argument from the Parashara Smriti)
